questions.stem: Humans have about 20,000 genes but more than 160,000 proteins. What mainly explains this?
questions.explanation: Alternative splicing produces several proteins from one gene. A: Pseudogenes don't make functional proteins. C: Gene families are separate genes. D: Housekeeping genes are a category, not a mechanism. E: These are repetitive elements, not a way one gene yields several proteins.

questions.stem: A sequence resembles an active gene but lacks introns and a promoter and ends in a poly(A) stretch. What is it?
questions.explanation: Processed pseudogenes arise by retrotransposition of mRNA, so they lack introns and promoters. A: Nonprocessed pseudogenes keep introns. B: Housekeeping genes are functional. C: Microsatellites are short tandem repeats. D: lncRNA genes are transcribed from promoters.

questions.stem: A forensic lab compares DNA from a crime scene with suspects. Which markers vary most usefully between individuals?
questions.explanation: STR repeat number varies among people, enabling human identification. B: Centromeric repeats aren't used for routine identification. C: SINEs are interspersed retrotransposed elements, not the identification markers. D: Housekeeping exons are highly conserved. E: Telomere sequence is identical across people.

questions.stem: Which RNA acts as the peptidyl transferase during translation and makes up ~80% of cellular RNA?
questions.explanation: rRNA is the catalytic and structural core of ribosomes. A: mRNA is ~3–7% of RNA. B: tRNA is ~10–15%. C: snRNA functions in splicing. E: miRNA regulates gene expression.

questions.stem: A regulatory RNA of 22 nucleotides reduces protein production from a target gene. What is its mechanism?

options.A: Binding complementary mRNA, which RISC then degrades or blocks
options.B: Methylating CpG islands in the target promoter
options.C: Guiding splicing of the target pre-mRNA
options.D: Remodeling chromatin as a capped, polyadenylated transcript
options.E: Acting as a peptidyl transferase on the ribosome

questions.explanation: miRNAs (18–25 nt) act by RNA interference: they bind complementary mRNA, and the RISC complex suppresses translation and promotes degradation. B: Promoter methylation isn't an miRNA function. C: Splicing involves snRNAs. D: That describes lncRNAs (>200 nt). E: Peptidyl transferase activity belongs to rRNA.

questions.stem: Normal fibroblasts stop dividing after a limited number of divisions, but a cancer cell line divides indefinitely while keeping its chromosome ends stable. Which enzyme activity is most likely increased?
questions.explanation: Telomerase adds TTAGGG repeats to chromosome ends; its activity is abundant in cancer and insufficient in aging. A: Ligase joins DNA fragments. B: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling. D: Primase makes RNA primers. E: RNase H removes primers.

questions.stem: A tandem repeat array consists of a 30-bp unit repeated about 100 times (3 kb). How is it classified?
questions.explanation: Minisatellites (VNTRs) have 10–100-bp units in 0.5–30-kb arrays. A: STRs have 2–5-bp units. B: SINEs are interspersed retrotransposed elements <500 bp, not tandem arrays. C: LINEs are ~6-kb interspersed elements. E: Telomeres are 6-bp TTAGGG repeats at chromosome ends.

questions.stem: In C0t analysis, denatured genomic DNA is allowed to reanneal. Which fraction renatures at the lowest C0t values?
questions.explanation: Reassociation rate is proportional to copy number, so highly repetitive satellite DNA renatures first (C0t <10⁻²). A: Unique sequences renature last (C0t 10–10⁴). C: Moderately repetitive DNA renatures at intermediate C0t (10⁻²–10). D: Mostly single-copy genes. E: Mostly single copies too.
